quotes.text: 2. 1514 onwards. Walls of brick, with freestone dressings. Roofs covered with lead, tiles and slates. Begun by Cardinal Wolsey, much of whose work survives particularly the ranges around the Base Court, the Clock Court and the Kitchen Court. King Henry VIII made extensive alterations between 1529-40, including the rebuilding of the Great Hall from 1532 the remodelling of the Chapel (1535-6) and building of Chapel Court. The extension of the kitchens and the addition of the projecting, turretted side wings to the west facade. Queen Elizabeth made some changes including the building of the privy kitchen but in 1689 William III began a major building campaign with Sir Christopher Wren as architect.

note: Tranche 3, English medieval fabric and the Tudor house, 5 Sep 2026. THE FLAGSHIP TUDOR EXEMPLAR'S LIST ENTRY STATES NOT ONE DIMENSION, NOT ONE STOREY COUNT AND NOT ONE BAY COUNT, so this record carries no measurements at all -- and that is the finding, not a gap in the research. Two extracts with different queries returned the same paragraph. The entry does not mention the diaper brickwork, the terracotta roundels or the chimney shafts that the node's own description makes this style's signature; it is an administrative list entry for a royal palace, not a description of it. The exemplar names two courts within the palace and Historic England lists the palace as one entry -- `oq/an-exemplar-that-is-not-one-whole-building`.
